title: Connected a multi-agent system (Gemini + GPT + Claude) directly to Blender  thoughts on 3D/game workflows?
author: Large-Explorer-8532
selftext:
Hey guys, Ive connected a multi-agent system (Gemini + GPT + Claude) directly to Blender  thoughts on 3D/game workflows?

Built a multi-agent setup where Gemini, GPT, and Claude interact directly with Blender the agent operates Blender the way a human would, so wireframes and meshes come out clean.

Im very very curious if anyone here sees this being useful in 3D game asset pipelines or other workflows. Would love your thoughts!

comments.body: Could you please share more info for who is totally beginner?

replies.author: Large-Explorer-8532
replies.body:
Yes of course. So it uses an MCP protocol to connect to Blender. It learns from Blender documentation how to use the software via APIs or sometimes the buttons/UI. It has an orchestrator agent that divides the workflow, created in langchain, into subagents and that is when Gemini + GPT + Claude comes cause each of them has a strenght compared to the other. Gemini for example is amazing understanding images. 

We created this UI so you can chat with it, it runs locally in your computer the app and connects to the agents LLM from your computer. It does not send your assets to the LLM. Let me know if that was too technical or not, happy to help :)

comments.author: Opening-West-4369
comments.body: what does this add over just running blender-mcp myself for free

replies.author: Large-Explorer-8532
replies.body:
Great question! blender-mcp is a fantastic open source project - shoutout to Siddhartha, he's doing great work. We're not competing, it really depends on what you need.  
  
\-blender-mcp: you bring your own API keys, host everything yourself, and you get full control. Perfect if you're already comfortable with that setup  
\-3D-Agent: multi-agent system (multiple models collaborating on a task), built-in UI, no API keys to manage. More plug-and-play.

The output quality also differs since we're running a multi-agent loop where the agents verify their own work at each step, but honestly both tools push Blender + AI forward and that's a good thing.

If you like open source and self-hosting, blender-mcp is solid. If you want something ready to go with a UI and don't want to manage APIs, that's where we come in.

replies.body:
thanks for your reply.  I think you could go further and add some better tooling than blender-mcp to distinguish.  for example the viewport capture tool could be improved & made more intelligent, e.g. if agent is working on a humanoid mesh, have a tool to capture screenshots from front-facing angle, back-facing angle, side view and compare.

just my 2 cents having only worked w blender-mcp

replies.author: Large-Explorer-8532
replies.body:
Ha, you're not wrong! that's definitely rough blocking, not a finished model. I'm a developer, not a 3D artist, so my skill level in Blender is honestly beginner at best.

But that's kind of the point... this is where the tool is at right now, and I think the interesting question is where it could go. If someone with actual modeling experience (like yourself) was driving it, the output would be a different story since you'd know what to ask for and how to refine it.

As someone who clearly knows their way around Blender, what would you actually want an AI assistant to handle? Or why not? The tedious stuff like UV unwrapping setup, repetitive modifiers, scene organization? Or is there no part of your workflow where this would save time?

replies.author: derleek
replies.body: I would not want a non deterministic algorithm doing any of the things you're proposing it's good for... even if it was free.  At best these tools will be used for concept art and thrown away.

replies.author: derleek
replies.body:
Great question.  Definitely looks like something I would never include in my games.  The website boasts some pretty egregious and arbitrary benefits...

  
"85% faster modeling, 3x faster iteration, "100% clean" wireframes."

Gonna need to see how these numbers were calculated.  You get 3 prompts a day... lol.  NOPE.  I can't imagine this being faster in any way.

replies.author: Large-Explorer-8532
replies.body:
Those were based on internal testing comparing repetitive tasks (scene setup, modifier stacking, basic blocking) vs doing them manually, not full production modeling. And that is for me. Definitely not claiming it replaces an experienced artist's workflow end to end.

The 3 prompts/day is the free tier which enough to test if it's useful for your specific workflow before committing. We're a small team and API costs add up fast, so that's the tradeoff for keeping it free to try.

Genuinely curious though what does your game asset pipeline look like? If there's a repetitive part of your workflow that eats time (like blocking out environments, setting up lighting rigs, batch operations), that's exactly where this kind of tool could slot in. Not replacing the craft, just automating the boring parts.

What engine are you working with?

replies.author: derleek
replies.body:
So completely made up and subjective numbers? Got it.  

No thanks.  I don't think these types of tools are going to save me any time right now.   Perhaps in several years, but I don't really want to clean up after AI; I like modeling.

**ALL of your plans have 3 prompts per day listed in pricing.**

replies.author: Large-Explorer-8532
replies.body:
The numbers came from timed internal testing on repetitive tasks... I explained that above. Not claiming it replaces a skilled artist's full workflow. On pricing good catch, that's a display bug. Paid tiers have way higher limits, and do not have any daily limit. Already fixed the info. 

what does "clean up after AI" look like for you? Because the output here is actual bpy operations and modifier stacks, not baked meshes. Clean wireframes. Curious what you'd expect to go wrong with those.

replies.author: derleek
replies.body:
furthermore I don't anyone should adopt a non deterministic tool for any of the things you are suggesting it for.  IMO you're going after the complete wrong market; embrace the vibe.  No serious professional will find this appealing at all.  Vibe slop slingers will probably find it novel if they can't set up these tools for themselves.

Besides is it not just a wrapper for a wrapper? I cannot see this working out for you.  Good luck tho!

Cheers.

replies.author: Large-Explorer-8532
replies.body:
Hey Derleek, Thank you for your inputs!  
  
So... Wrapper for a wrapper is a over simplification of the whole economy. By that logic Stripe is a wrapper for banks and Figma is a wrapper for rendering engines. The value is in what it abstracts away. The agent reads the viewport, writes bpy code, applies modifiers, and verifies the result visually across multiple models. That's orchestration, not passthrough. Will that be good enough? I dont know!! Probably not!  
  
Fair point on determinism, and I'd agree you wouldn't put this at the end of a production pipeline. But for blocking, iteration, scene setup? You're adjusting the output anyway. Fast rough draft, not final deliverable.

You mean 3D market? Indie game? But the indie devs and solo creators burning 4 hours on environment blocking seem to disagree. What would it take for you to consider a tool like this useful?

replies.author: derleek
replies.body:
Reducing stripe to a wrapper is 100% false.  Stripe is it's own payment processing gateway; they are not subject to the same business / cost model that you are in any way shape or form.  I feel like this is some line that's passed around by the numerous other startups doing exactly what you're doing and it doesn't hold up to any scrutiny at all.  The entire economy is a wrapper? GTFO dude.  Quit drinking the koolaid.

Modeling is art.  I don't believe automating it in this manner is not what artists should seek to do.  There are many... MANY established ways to reduce the time we spend doing what we do.  They should seek mastery of their craft.  Taking these shortcuts is a mistake in multiple ways.  Applying these tools for things that we need to work reliably the same time is also not what people should be doing.  

There is nothing you can do to make this compelling to me, personally.  Why would I invest in renting this tech when I could be running my own models locally with tools I own, not renting an api wrapper for a wrapper.

replies.author: Large-Explorer-8532
replies.body:
That is exactly my point, the economy is not just a wrapper and that is a limited view and over simplifcation of things :)

On mastery... fully respect that, and I agree modeling is art. But even master painters don't stretch their own canvases anymore. The craft is in the creative decisions, not the repetitive setup.

Have you hosted a model locally? What was your experience with its capabilities and hardware? I find it pretty challenging to have good results with it. Maybe you have 128gb of GPU available to host big models, I do not. Smaller ones are bad at coding for now,  
  
And I'm not trying to convince you. I'm just trying to understand your perspective because it helps us build a better product. You clearly know your stuff, which is exactly why the pushback is valuable. Thank you!

replies.author: derleek
replies.body: you are trying to convince me ;)  It's just not going how you thought it would. I've given you enough of my time and you know how I feel about your product.

comments.author: beam123
comments.body: so other than being an add-on, how is this different than [Nativeblend](http://nativeblend.app)?

replies.author: Large-Explorer-8532
replies.body:
Good question! I actually like what Nativeblend is doing but have not used them much. But more tools pushing 3D + AI forward is a good thing.

The main difference is that 3D-Agent is more like a Copilot for Blender than a one-shot generation tool. It's not about generating a single asset... it stays with you inside Blender across your whole workflow. Want to adjust the camera? Rig a character? Try an animation? You just ask.

We're also 100% focused on Blender, not cloud-based 3D generation.

One thing that surprised us, some of our users started using it to predict how renders would look before waiting several minutes per frame. Just ask the agent to set up the scene and check the viewport and to understand and "predict" how that frame would look like.

Have you tried both? Would be curious to hear how they compare from a user perspective.
